title: Slow Productivity
author: Cal Newport
blurb: Cal Newport argues that modern knowledge work never settled on a real definition of productivity. Without one, people fell back on visible activity, like fast email replies, packed calendars and constant meetings, as a stand-in for real accomplishment. He calls this pseudo-productivity and says it drives the burnout so many professionals feel. As an alternative, he offers slow productivity, built on three principles. First, do fewer things, because every commitment carries hidden overhead that crowds out real progress. Second, work at a natural pace, on longer time horizons and with seasonal variation, the way many great thinkers of the past did. Third, obsess over quality, because work that is truly excellent earns the leverage to protect a calmer way of working. The result is a sustainable path to meaningful results without exhaustion.

lessons.b: Because knowledge work never defined productivity, we treat looking busy as a stand-in for real accomplishment, and that is burning us out.
Knowledge workers lost the clear measures of factory work, so emails, meetings and fast replies became the default signal of value.
Every project brings an overhead tax of coordination and communication, so taking on fewer commitments lets each one move faster and better.
Limit missions, projects and daily tasks, and use systems that pull in new work only when you have capacity, instead of letting requests pile on.
Many great thinkers of the past worked slowly over years, so set longer timelines and avoid making every day an urgent sprint.
